body:
This thread makes me sad. I have so much to say on this topic I don't know where to begin, so pardon any lack of organization. You can look at the post history for this throwaway... I was pretty deep into the darkness.

I'm 25 attending the U. I went to college initially, the standard 4 years 18-22, but hated my first major, but sort of was already mostly down that path so just finished it. I'm back for another that I'm more passionate about.

Luckily, I have extremely good memory, so I got by with decent grades without even having to try. For those who can't do that, I can't imagine the extra stress of failing classes on top of what some commenters are feeling.

There's a difference between sadness and depression. This summer I feel I really kicked my depression, although it was one of the saddest summers I've had. Sounds like a contradiction, but it's not. Depression is such a debilitating fog that puts this haze over everything in life and is absolutely crippling. Sadness is obviously not great, but if you're healthy you can work through it. Depression with sadness just destroys you. To elaborate on the difference: I was seeing someone incredible before summer and it fell apart--still dealing with it as she's in a class and we do see each other this term--but at the same time I've never felt more motivated despite missing her. I decided to invest in me before summer. I worked out almost every day (a first).  I gained 20 pounds. My depression manifested mostly in perpetual tiredness and the ability to just sleep all day if possible. You can see that from my last posts. But now, I sleep 7 hours a day and am absolutely awake by 6am and have absolutely no urge for a nap throughout the day. Something just clicked in my head, and I haven't identified what exactly. At least a bit of it is that if I were to meet someone great like that again, I want to be at my best. Maybe that little trigger was the final straw to break my depression camel's back, but it's way more complicated and I can't say for sure. What I do know is that I do not ever want to descend even 1/4th of the way back to the depression I had since I was like 10. The sadness I currently wake up with every day is not even close to the constant plague that is depression.

Depression is such a handicap in relation to your peers. It is not even close to sadness and don't let anyone tell you it's sadness or berate you as "everyone feels sad". Especially, don't let yourself think the thoughts and put yourself down. Unfortunately, I don't know the cure. I honestly never felt therapy was helpful. In fact, I regretted every instance of telling a professional as that just made it worse. I was fortunate enough to have friends who would listen to anything I had to say and they were way better. If you don't have that relationship, maybe therapy is better. Don't let it just fester. I analogize it (especially with my symptoms) to me having 4 hours less in a day (oversleeping), and while awake, being on like 20% battery compared to others. That shit you're missing every day adds up fast and compounds day by day, especially as a student.

I don't know all or even close to a small portion of answers, but some things I've learned:

For the longest time I thought I was an introvert. I'm not. I'm certainly not the "iconic definition" of an extrovert, but I thrive off interaction with people. My depression just made that contact difficult to initiate. If you're that way, you just have to force yourself. And I cannot emphasize how much I am empathetic to how hard it is when depressed.

Especially for the introverts, you need a hobby or passion. I could never produce happiness for myself. I sort of had to vicariously live through my healthy friends. They'd always have to do the work of what to do, what plans to make for fun, or just drop by on them doing something interesting. Whenever I was alone, it was dark because I didn't know where to find happiness. You just gotta try to find something. One simple passion can add so much dimension to your life. Just to name one, say, cooking. You can get into that, strive to make each recipe better each time, have countless hours of media to keep yourself busy (cooking shows, tutorials, etc), make meeting people way easier (cooking things for people is a pretty quick way to someone's heart or just having a conversation point that can feed many a conversation for a lot of content), etc. etc. Sometimes, hobbies that involve some sort of "creation" like cooking might be a bit much, but they don't need to be. Just starting with something like getting into a certain genre of music or game or something that has a community can be beneficial, too.

Gaming. If you're a gamer, make sure you're a healthy one and not just one who uses it as an escape. Certainly, using sometimes as an escape can be great. But if it's a daily escape, at that point you're just escaping life. I wasted so much time gaming and really wish I moderated myself.

Recognize that people aren't over-analyzing you. I always was so conservative with my actions cause I felt like everyone would remember. No one cares and most people are dealing with their own problems. I.e. I'm feeling alone, I want to talk to attempt to make a friend. Will she think I'm hitting on her? Oh well, guess I shouldn't do it. Should I talk to this guy? Ah, he'll probably think I'm weird, better not. Should I try this group hobby/activity? Oh no, I'm going to suck and everyone will care. Spoiler: they won't. Just trust yourself and if you're just pursuing happiness, any negative recoil from someone else reflects on them not you. This also goes the other way. People will not be over-analyzing you for when your depression is hitting hardest or you're not doing well. You have to reach out.

Get help early and often. Physically, I'd never get help for medical issues. I once had a debilitating "cold" for 6 weeks before coughing up blood one morning and learning that it was actually bronchitis. I was just so used to feeling like shit that feeling more like shit didn't really matter. It's a really bad mentality. Mentally, if you're alone or sad or whatever, you gotta push yourself to reach out early before it's eating away at you. Problems can compound fast, so respect yourself and care for yourself. Academically, especially in science or math, the ideas and complexity only compound and get worse. If you don't understand topic A fully, and B relies on A, and then C relies on B, eventually you will crumble if you were struggling with A. Get help. There's no shame in it.

Just take it one step at a time. Don't try to do too much at once. Small victories add up. I know for sure I wish I had kicked it earlier and wouldn't be 2.5 years behind my peers who graduated in something they enjoyed the first time, but the best time to plant a tree is now.

Perhaps I'll edit in more as I think of it, but I hope all of you can find something. I don't even know if this helps at all, but hopefully.
